sentence: Twelve minutes. The submission portal closes at midnight and the final section is still two paragraphs short. My hands are shaking on the keyboard. Save, save, save. Why does the cursor keep skipping. I keep retyping the same sentence and it sounds worse each time. Eleven minutes now. There is no time to re-read. There is no time to think. Just words, any words, into the box and click submit before the clock turns over.

Three minutes until the proposal has to be in the partner's inbox. The PDF is still exporting. The progress bar has not moved. I refresh. It freezes. I am going to lose my job. My pulse is in my ears now. Two minutes. Force quit. Re-open. Re-export. Please. Please. Please.

The grant cycle ends at five and my advisor still has not signed the cover sheet. I am sprinting across the quad. My laptop bag is hitting my back with every step. If she is not in her office I do not know what I will do. Four-fifty. The building door is heavier than I remember. Stairs, take the stairs, the elevator is too slow.

Final exam, eighteen minutes left, three essay questions untouched. Skip the long one. Skip it. Bullet points count for partial credit. Write anything. The proctor is walking the aisles. My handwriting has gone illegible. I cannot remember the years of the Treaty. Make up a year. Just make up a year and move on.

The auction closes in ninety seconds and the bid page will not load. Refresh. Nothing. Refresh. Nothing. I am going to lose the apartment. Sixty seconds. The wheel is still spinning. Why now, of all the moments in the day, why now. My finger is hovering over the trackpad like it can make the network faster.

Tax filing deadline. Eleven fifty-three at night. The software wants a verification code that should have come three minutes ago. Check spam. Check trash. Resend. Resend. Resend. The IRS does not care that the email server is slow. The penalty stacks per day. I am refreshing my inbox with one hand and my eyes are starting to blur.

Five minutes to the end of the trading session and the order is hung. The confirmation will not come through. The market is moving against me by the second. Cancel. Resubmit. The platform is asking me to log in again. I am going to be down six figures by the time this clears.

Conference abstract closes at noon UTC. It is eleven fifty-eight. I am still fixing the title because autocorrect mangled a word and now the field will not accept my edit. The character counter is red. Cut a word. Cut another word. The page has no time to wait for me to be eloquent.

The court filing window shuts at four. It is three fifty-one. The clerk's email bounced. The fax machine is making a noise I have never heard. My paralegal is on hold with the help line. Nine minutes. Nine minutes and the entire case is procedurally dead.

Eight minutes before the visa portal closes for the cycle. The upload field is rejecting my passport scan because the file is somehow too large now, after it was fine yesterday. Compress it. Lower the resolution. The clock keeps moving. I have rehearsed this submission for six weeks and it is going to die on a file size.

Gate B47. The board says CLOSED in red. I am running. The wheels of my carry-on are screaming on the tile. Sorry, sorry, excuse me. I can see the jet bridge. The agent is reaching for the door. Wait. Wait. Please. My ticket is still loading on my phone. The signal in this terminal is garbage. I am waving a blank screen at her.

Security line is wrapped twice around the stanchions. My flight boards in twenty-three minutes. The TSA officer is moving in slow motion. I do not have time to be polite. Excuse me, excuse me, is there a faster line. The man in front of me is unpacking his entire bag for a water bottle he forgot. I want to scream.

The shuttle from long-term parking is sitting at the wrong terminal. Driver, please, this is the wrong terminal. I have a flight. He shrugs. I am opening the door at a red light and running across four lanes of dropoff traffic. A horn blares. I do not look. The departures sign keeps blinking.

Final boarding call for flight 1142 to Frankfurt. That is me. That is me. I am still at customs. The agent is reading my landing card line by line. Sir. Sir. My plane. He does not look up. There is no version of this where I do not miss the connection. My whole onward itinerary is collapsing.

The transfer in Doha is forty-five minutes and I have already burned thirty of it in the immigration queue. The next gate is in a different terminal. There is a train. I do not know which train. I am scanning the signage and the Arabic is gorgeous and useless to me right now. Run. Just run.

My passport. Where is my passport. I had it at the kiosk. It is not in my back pocket. It is not in my jacket. It is not in the front pouch of the bag. Oh god. The line behind me is six people deep and they all see it on my face. I am going to be the person who held everyone up.

Departure board updated. Gate change. From B12 to D44. That is a forty minute walk in a normal airport. Boarding in fourteen minutes. I am already running before my brain has caught up to the new letter. People are pulling their kids out of my way. I have never moved this fast in dress shoes.

The agent at the desk is shaking her head. The flight is closed. I can see it through the window. The jet bridge is still attached. Please. Please call them. There is one seat. I know there is one seat. My voice is too loud. People are looking. I do not care. I cannot be here tomorrow.

Boarding group six is called and my child is in the bathroom. Has been in there for nine minutes. I am knocking. Buddy. Buddy. The agent at the desk is glancing at me. We are the last two unscanned tickets. I do not know if I should leave the bag, leave the gate, knock the door down.

The Uber is stuck. The driver keeps saying five minutes. He has said five minutes for twenty minutes. My terminal is three exits away and traffic is not moving. I can see the planes climbing out. One of those is mine. One of those was supposed to be mine.

She was right here. She was holding the edge of the cart. I turned for two seconds. The cereal aisle is empty. I am calling her name. Other shoppers are turning. Maya. Maya. The fluorescent lights are too bright. My voice is getting higher. I do not recognize my own voice. Where is she. Where is she.

Code Adam over the loudspeaker. My code. They are saying his name. Three years old, red shirt, blue shoes. I gave them the description and now it sounds like a missing child poster. I am running aisle to aisle. The store has never looked this big. Every blue shoe in the world is somewhere in here except his.

The toy section. He has to be in the toy section. He is not in the toy section. I am pushing carts out of my way. A woman asks if I am okay. I cannot answer. My mouth is open and nothing comes out. I am thinking about the parking lot. The doors of this store open straight onto a parking lot.

Security pulls up the camera. There. There she is. Aisle nine, eleven minutes ago, holding hands with someone. Who is that. I cannot see the face. I cannot see her face. The guard is rewinding and I want him to go faster. Faster. Just play it forward. Just show me where she is right now.

I lock eyes with a teenage employee. Have you seen a little boy. About this tall. Curly hair. He blinks at me. I am repeating myself. Curly hair. Curly hair. He starts to answer and I am already gone, running, because he gestured vaguely toward the back of the store and I cannot wait for the rest of the sentence.

Every exit. Watch every exit. I am at the front of the store telling the manager to lock the doors and she is asking me to calm down. I cannot calm down. He is four. He is four. I am going to find him in the next ninety seconds or I am going to come apart in front of all these strangers.

He is not answering. He always answers. I am calling his name in the voice he listens to and he is not answering. The mall is full of music and laughing kids and none of them are mine. I am turning in a slow circle in the middle of the food court and the world is tilting.

The dressing room attendant says she did not see anyone go in alone. The whole rack of dresses I last saw him near is a wall of fabric now and I am yanking each one aside like he might be folded behind it. He is not. He is not. My chest is so tight I am barely breathing.

A clerk picks her up at the customer service desk and pages me. I am running and crying at the same time and the store is going by in a blur. She is sitting on the counter eating a lollipop and she looks up like nothing happened. I am on my knees holding her. I cannot stop shaking.

Ten minutes. He has been missing for ten minutes. I am cataloguing what he was wearing. Green pants. Or was it the dinosaur shirt. I cannot remember what I dressed him in this morning. How do I not know this. The security guy needs a description and I am giving him three different shirts.

Smoke alarm. Smoke alarm. The hallway is full of grey. I cannot see the door at the end of it. I am crawling. Stay low. Stay low. Where is the dog. The dog. I am calling her and the smoke is going in my throat. The floor is hot. I am at the top of the stairs and the stairs look wrong, they look wrong, there is light coming up from the bottom of them.

The kitchen. Oil fire. I left the pan. I left the pan on. The flames are up the cabinets. I am screaming for everyone to get out. Get out. Get out. The smoke detector is shrieking. I am throwing a lid at the pan and missing. Where is the baking soda. Where is the baking soda. Just go. Just go. Leave it.

Three a.m. Smoke. Pulling my partner out of bed by his arm. He is groggy and I am dragging him. The smoke is in the room already. The kids. The kids. We split. He goes left. I go right. I am banging on doors. Wake up wake up wake up. The hallway light is gone. Power is out.

Front door is hot. Do not open it. Do not open it. Back door. Back door. Climbing over the couch. The smoke is settling lower than my head now. I am holding a wet dish towel to my mouth. I have always read that you do that. I never thought I would do that. The latch is sticking. Why is the latch sticking.

We are out. We are on the lawn. I am counting heads. One. Two. Three. Where is four. Where is four. He was right behind me. I am running back toward the door and the firefighter is grabbing me by the shoulders and saying ma'am ma'am and I am not stopping. He is in there.

The window. The bedroom window. I cannot get it open. The frame has been painted shut for a decade. I am hitting the latch with the heel of my shoe. The smoke is pushing into the room from under the door. I can see it. I can see it like a slow grey snake. The shoe is not working. Get the chair. Get the chair.

Roof. The roof is the only way out. The fire escape is engulfed. I am at the top of the apartment building in my socks and a tee shirt and the firefighters are below me with a ladder that does not look long enough. They are yelling something. I cannot hear over the sirens. They want me to jump. They want me to jump.

The cat. The cat is under the bed. I am on my stomach reaching and the smoke is at the ceiling and dropping by the second. Come here. Come here. She is hissing. She is hissing at me. I have ten seconds. I do not have ten seconds. I am sobbing and grabbing whatever fur I can.

Phone. Where is my phone. I need to call 911. The flames are at the curtain. I am patting my pockets and they are empty and I do not even remember where I left it. Just go. Just go. Call from outside. From the neighbor. From anywhere. Move.

The basement furnace exploded. I felt it through the floor. The whole house jumped. I am pulling the kids off the couch and we are running for the front door and I do not even have shoes on. Outside. Outside. Get to the street. Get away from the windows. The windows could go any second.

911. He is not breathing. He is not breathing. I do not know how long. He was on the floor. I came in and he was on the floor. The dispatcher is asking me his age and I cannot remember if he is fifty-two or fifty-three. I cannot remember. Hurry. Please. Just send someone.

She is seizing. On the kitchen floor. She is seizing. I am on hands and knees holding her head off the tile. The phone is on speaker. The voice is telling me not to put anything in her mouth. I am crying and saying I know I know I know. How long has this been. I have lost track.

Allergic reaction. The EpiPen. I cannot find the EpiPen. Her face is swelling. Her lips are swelling. I am tearing through the bag. Where did I put it. I always put it in the side pocket. It is not in the side pocket. The dispatcher is talking. I am not listening. Find it find it find it.

The address. What is my address. I am standing in my own house and I am blanking on the number. Two something. Two two something. The 911 operator is patient. I am not. There is a man on the floor and I do not know my own house number. The street. I know the street. I am yelling the street name.

Chest pain. Left arm. He is grey. He is grey. I am dialing with one hand and unlocking the front door with the other so the paramedics can get in fast. Aspirin. The bottle is in the bathroom. I am sprinting up the stairs and the dispatcher is asking me questions and I am not answering, I am running.

The baby. The baby is blue. I am doing the back blows. The video on the phone showed back blows. Between the shoulder blades. Hard. Harder than feels right. Five. Five back blows and then chest thrusts. My hands are too big for her body. I am too rough I am too rough I am going to break her.

Bleeding. He cut his leg with the chainsaw. There is so much blood. So much. I am pressing a towel down and the towel is already soaked. Another towel. Another towel. The dispatcher says fifteen minutes for the ambulance and I am screaming that he does not have fifteen minutes.

Stroke. I think it is a stroke. Her face. One side of her face. She cannot raise her arm. The acronym. FAST. F A S T. Face, arm, speech, time. Time. Time is the one that matters and we are losing it. I have her hand and I am keeping her talking and her words are coming out wrong.

He overdosed. I think he overdosed. He is not waking up. I am shaking his shoulders. Wake up. Wake up. The naloxone. Where is the naloxone. I am tearing open the package with my teeth because my hands are shaking too hard. Up the nose. Up the nose. The instructions said up the nose.

She fell. She fell off the ladder. Her leg is bent the wrong way. She is screaming. I cannot move her. I am not supposed to move her. The dispatcher is telling me to keep her still and I am holding her down because she is trying to sit up and the bone is sticking through the skin and I am not going to throw up I am not going to throw up.

The truck did not stop. The truck did not stop. I am pulling onto the shoulder and my hands will not let go of the wheel. Get out. Get out and check. The other driver is moving. He is moving. Someone is screaming. I think the screaming is me. Glass everywhere. Glass in my lap. My phone is in the footwell and I cannot reach it.

Black ice. The back end is sliding. I am steering into it and it is not catching. The guardrail is coming up fast. Brake brake brake. Do not brake. Which one. Which one. I cannot remember. Impact. Airbag. The world goes white and then there is the smell of burning plastic and I am upside down.

I hit a deer. I hit a deer and now the engine is smoking and I am on a country road with no signal and the deer is moving on the shoulder. Oh god it is still alive. I am crying and dialing and the call is failing. Get away from the car. The hood is smoking. What if it catches.

The car in front slammed on the brakes and I rear ended them and the car behind me rear ended me and we are all on the freeway in three lanes of seventy mile an hour traffic. Get out. Hazards on. Get to the shoulder. Run. Cars are still coming. They are not slowing down. They are not slowing down.

My daughter was in the back seat. She is crying. That is good. Crying is good. Crying means breathing. I am unbuckling and trying to get to her and my own door is jammed. Climb over the console. Climb. The car seat looks fine. She looks fine. Please be fine please be fine please be fine.

The motorcycle is down. The motorcycle is down ten feet from my hood. I did not see him. He came out of the blind spot. I am running across the intersection with my hands shaking and people are honking at me and I am yelling do not move do not move and he is not moving anyway.

Smell of gasoline. Strong. Too strong. The tank must be cracked. Get everyone out. Get everyone out now. I am unbuckling the kids and the door will only open halfway. Squeeze through. The smell is getting worse. Get back. Get back from the car. How far is far enough.

The other driver is getting out of his car and walking toward me and he is yelling. I do not know what happened. I think the light was green. I think it was green. He is in my face. My hands are up. I just need to call someone. Just let me call someone. My phone is somewhere on the road.

Hit and run. He hit me and kept going. License plate. License plate. I am trying to read it as he disappears. I am repeating it out loud. Three letters then four numbers. Four numbers. Repeat repeat repeat until I can type it. Do not lose it. Do not lose it.

I rolled the truck. I rolled the truck off the embankment. The roof is the floor. The floor is the ceiling. The seatbelt is the only thing holding me. Unbuckle and I drop. Do not unbuckle. Do not unbuckle. The engine is ticking. Something is dripping. I am alone out here and no one saw it happen.

Production is down. Down. Every second is money bleeding out and the on-call pager won't stop screaming. I'm SSHing into the box, fingers slipping, typing the wrong password twice. The CEO is in the channel asking what's happening. I don't know what's happening. Logs are flooding past faster than I can read. Something about memory, something about a deadlock. Restart the service. No, get the dump first. No, just restart, we need it up. My heart is pounding so hard I can feel it in my teeth.

Database connections at 100%. Can't get a read. Can't get a write. The dashboard is solid red across every region. Slack notifications stacking up faster than I can dismiss them. Engineering VP just joined the call. Where is the runbook. Where IS the runbook. I had it open ten minutes ago.

Kill the deploy. Kill it now. The new build is OOM-killing every pod and we're cascading. I can see the graph going vertical. Rolling back. Why is the rollback hanging. Why is it hanging. Twelve thousand users on the error page right now and the number is climbing.

Someone pushed straight to main. Straight to main, no review, no canary. Now the payment service is throwing 500s on every request. I'm trying to revert but the CI is queued behind seventeen other jobs. Cancel them all. Force-push the previous SHA. My hands are shaking.

Etcd is split-brain. We have two leaders. Two. I'm watching the cluster eat itself in real time. Every write is being rejected on one side and accepted on the other and we are about to have completely divergent state. Stop the writes. STOP THE WRITES.

The cert expired. The cert expired and nobody renewed it and now every API call from every customer is failing. Auto-renewal was supposed to run. It didn't run. I'm trying to issue a new one manually but Let's Encrypt is rate-limiting us because we hit it too many times trying to fix it.

Disk full. Disk is at 100% on the primary. Logs are not rotating. Why are the logs not rotating. The cron is missing. The cron is just not there. Deleting old files by hand, ls, rm, ls, rm, every second the queue is backing up further. Customers are screaming on Twitter.

Replication lag is six hours and climbing. Six hours. The read replicas are serving stale data and we just shipped an order confirmation to a customer for a product we already sold out of. How many. How many customers got the wrong page. I need to pull a query and I need to pull it now.
DNS is broken. DNS. Of all the things. I can't even SSH in because the bastion hostname won't resolve. The IP. What's the IP. I should have memorized the IP. Why didn't I memorize the IP.

We are being DDoSed. Right now. Traffic is twenty times normal and every layer is buckling. CDN is shedding load. Origin is on fire. I'm trying to push the WAF rule but the dashboard itself is timing out because the dashboard runs on the same infra.

Twenty minutes left. Twenty. I haven't even started the essay question and I just realized I misread the prompt for the first section. Did I answer the wrong question entirely. Flipping back. Yes. Yes I did. My stomach is in my throat and I can hear the proctor's footsteps and someone two rows over just turned in their paper.

I forgot the formula. I knew this formula last night. I drilled it. It is GONE. Completely gone, like it was never in my head at all. Pencil hovering, blank space, blank brain. Move on. Move on, come back. But I can't move on because the next problem uses the same formula.

The Scantron. I bubbled the wrong row. I bubbled the wrong row for the last fifteen questions. Erasing. Erasing faster. The eraser is smearing and tearing little flakes into the bubbles and I cannot get them clean and the timer is going and my hands won't stop shaking.

Bar exam. Day two. My laptop just blue-screened. Mid-essay. I had three pages written and the screen is solid blue with a sad face on it and the proctor is walking toward me looking confused and I am about to lose my entire legal career to a Windows update.

I parked in the wrong lot. The MCAT is starting in eleven minutes and I parked at the wrong building and now I am sprinting across campus with my backpack flapping and my ID badge swinging and I cannot remember which way the testing center is and every building looks the same.

Five minutes left and I have not even looked at section three. Five minutes. Flipping pages. Reading nothing. Just bubbling. C, C, B, C, A, anything, please, just put something down for every question.

I left the cheat sheet in the bathroom. I left it on the counter. The proctor went into the bathroom after me. Did they see it. Did they SEE IT. I am about to be expelled and I cannot focus on a single problem because I am waiting for the tap on the shoulder.

Pencils down in thirty seconds. Thirty. I have one essay left and a conclusion to write and I am writing as fast as my hand will let me and the words are coming out as scribbles and I cannot even read my own handwriting back.

Wait. Wait. The date on the cover is wrong. This is last year's exam. This is the wrong exam. Am I in the wrong room. Looking around. Everyone else has the same booklet. So this IS the right one and they just printed the wrong year. Don't think about it don't think about it just start writing.

I left the calculator in the car. The car is in the garage three blocks away. The proctor said no leaving and re-entering. The first problem is a derivative I can do in my head but problem two needs the calculator and I am already behind and oh god oh god think think think.

GPS just rerouted us through downtown and we are sitting at a red light watching the minutes tick over and my sister is supposed to walk down the aisle in nineteen minutes and we are still six miles away. The driver is honking. Everyone is honking. Nothing is moving. I am the maid of honor. I have the rings.
Dress is unzipping itself in the back of the Uber. The zipper broke. The whole bodice is gaping open and the wedding is in twenty minutes and the bride is texting me asking where I am.

Forgot the marriage license. Forgot. The. License. We are pulling into the church and my brother just realized it is sitting on the kitchen counter in the apartment and the ceremony starts in eight minutes and you literally cannot get married without it.

The limo broke down. On the highway. With the bride in it. In her dress. The driver is looking under the hood and shaking his head and the bride is crying and the wedding planner is on the phone screaming and I do not know how we get her to the venue in fifteen minutes.
Officiant just texted that he is stuck in traffic on the bridge. The ceremony starts in twelve minutes. Who else can do this. Who in this room is ordained. Anyone. Anyone.

My speech. My speech is on a phone that is at four percent battery and the cable does not fit any of the chargers in this building and the toasts start in nineteen minutes and I cannot remember a single line of what I wrote.

I am parking. I am running. Heels in one hand, bouquet in the other, hair coming undone, mascara already on my cheek. Through the parking lot. Past the cars. The double doors are right there. They are starting the music. They are starting the music NOW.

Ring bearer just dropped the ring. Into the grate. Into the storm drain. We can SEE it down there. The ceremony is in seven minutes. Somebody get a coat hanger. Somebody get anything. The groom does not know yet and I refuse to be the one to tell him.

Wrong venue. We drove to the wrong venue. The ceremony is at the OTHER vineyard, twenty minutes south, and the GPS pulled us to the one with the same name and we are standing in an empty parking lot with the wedding party in tuxedos and bridesmaid dresses staring at a closed-for-the-season sign.

Hairdresser is forty-five minutes late. The photographer is here. The mother of the bride is here. The bride is half-done with hair sticking out every direction and the first look is supposed to happen in eighteen minutes and the woman is not picking up her phone.

The storm is supposed to make landfall in nine hours and the gas station is out of gas. Both gas stations in town are out. The line at the third one is around the block and the tanker hasn't shown up and we still have to load the dog and grandma and the cat and we have not boarded a single window.
Mandatory evacuation order just came through the radio. Mandatory. They are not waiting. The bridge closes at six. The bridge is the only way out. It is four-thirty. We have not packed.

Water is already in the street. Up to the curb. Faster than they said it would be. The rain hasn't even started yet and I am throwing photo albums into a trash bag and the kids are crying because they want their stuffed animals and I cannot find the cat.

Highway is bumper to bumper for forty miles. Forty. We have been moving at five miles an hour for three hours and the storm is closing in behind us and the gas gauge is past the E and the nearest exit is in nine miles.

Plywood. We need plywood NOW. The Home Depot has been picked clean. The Lowe's is closing in twenty minutes. There is one sheet left at the hardware store across town and three people are heading there. I am driving with one hand and dialing with the other and asking them to please please hold it for me.

Generator won't start. Won't start. Pulled the cord nine times and nothing and the lights just flickered for the third time tonight and the freezer is full of food my parents froze last summer and if the power dies we lose all of it and the kids are scared and I cannot get this thing to start.

Mom won't leave. She won't leave the house. The storm surge is supposed to be twelve feet and her front door is six feet above sea level and I am on the phone begging her and she is telling me she has been through worse and there is no worse than this, there is no worse than this.

Trees are already coming down two streets over. We can hear them. Each one is a crack and a long groan and then the impact. The dog is hiding under the bed. I cannot get him out and the SUV is loaded and we need to leave now, NOW.

Hotel after hotel saying no vacancy. Eight calls so far. We are driving into the dark with two kids in the back and no destination and the weather radio keeps saying the storm has shifted west, west toward us, and every shelter we pass has a line snaking out the door.

Forgot the medications. All of them. Dad's blood pressure, Mom's insulin, my anxiety meds. They are all on the kitchen counter and we are an hour out and the storm is six hours out and if I turn around I might not get back across the bridge and if I don't turn around Dad's blood pressure is going to spike before this is over.

Down twelve percent at the open. Twelve. I am watching my retirement evaporate in real time and the broker's website keeps timing out every time I try to log in and I cannot even place a sell order because the order book is moving faster than the screen can refresh.

Margin call. Margin call email just came through. They want forty-seven thousand dollars by end of day or they liquidate the entire position at whatever it trades for. The market is down nine percent. The position is down twenty. I do not have forty-seven thousand dollars in cash.

Circuit breaker tripped at the seven percent mark. Trading halted for fifteen minutes. Fifteen minutes of staring at the screen with my heart hammering and the futures still falling and knowing that when it reopens it is going to be worse.

My phone has not stopped ringing since the bell. Clients. Every client. Each one wants to know what to do and I do not know what to do and I cannot tell them I do not know because I am supposed to be the one with the answers and the screens are red across every sector.

I just saw my own stop loss get blown through. Blown straight through with no fill. The order is sitting unexecuted because there is no bid anywhere near my stop and the price is in free fall and I am about to lose three years of savings in the next four minutes.

Compliance just emailed. They want positions flat by close. Every position. I have eighty open trades across forty-two symbols and the market is broken and the bid-ask spreads are wider than the daily range and I have four hours to unwind everything without blowing the book up further.

The boss is at my desk. Standing right behind me. He has not said a word, he is just watching the red numbers tick down and breathing through his nose and I can feel him there and I cannot think with him there and the position is bleeding faster every second.

Bloomberg just flashed that the bank failed. The bank. Our exposure to that bank is everything. Everything. I have to call the head of risk in the next sixty seconds and I do not know what the number is, I do not know how big our position is, I am pulling up the report and the report will not load.

Down twenty-two percent. Just kept selling. Just kept selling and now I am sitting here looking at a P&L that does not seem real and my hands are cold and I think I am going to be sick and there is still an hour left in the trading day.

Wife is calling. Wife is calling and she just saw the news and she is asking if we lost the down payment for the house and I do not have time to answer and the answer is yes and I have to keep working because if I stop right now we lose even more.

School just called. School just called and said something about a fall and they are calling an ambulance and they could not tell me how bad it is and I am in the car already and the seatbelt is not buckled and I do not care and I am running yellows and I will run reds if I have to.

Forty-five minutes from the hospital. Forty-five. The text said come now. Come now. What does come now mean. Is he. Is he still. I cannot ask. I cannot type with these hands. The exit is in two miles. Move. Move.

I am six lanes over from my exit. Six. The truck won't let me in. The Camry won't let me in. Signal on, signal on harder, the exit is right there and I am about to miss it and the next one is fourteen miles and my dad is in the ICU.

Construction. There is construction on the highway and I am sitting in stopped traffic and I can see the hospital tower in the distance and I cannot get to it and my sister is calling again, calling again, and I cannot pick up because I cannot hear what she is going to say.
Hospital parking garage is full. FULL. I am circling level after level and there is nowhere and I just abandoned the car on the curb by the emergency room entrance and I do not care if they tow it.

Running through the lobby. The information desk is asking my name. I am asking for the trauma wing. They are asking me to spell my name. SPELL MY NAME. I am spelling my name. Where is my mother. Where is she.

She fell. The neighbor found her. The neighbor called the ambulance and the neighbor called me and the ambulance went to St. Mary's not Sacred Heart and I just pulled into Sacred Heart and I have to drive twenty more minutes and I do not know if she is conscious.

Tank is on E. I cannot stop for gas. I cannot. The light has been on for fifteen miles and the hospital is twenty miles away and if I run out on the shoulder I will not be there in time and I do not know what in time means but I know I have to be there.

Rain is coming down so hard I cannot see the lane lines. Wipers on max. Still cannot see. The truck ahead has hazards on. The exit sign is a blur. My mother is in surgery and I am driving forty in a sixty-five and praying.

I cannot find my partner. The party was four of us and three are accounted for and the fourth is gone and his beacon is not coming through, not coming through, and the battery indicator on my unit just dropped to red.

Cell signal one bar. One. I am punching at the satellite messenger and the message will not send and the helicopter does not know where to go and the storm is rolling in and the visibility is dropping and the patient is fading.

We are live in three. Three. The chyron is wrong, the prompter just froze, the producer is talking in my earpiece and I cannot hear what she is saying and the floor manager is counting down with his fingers and I am the only person who is supposed to be talking in fifteen seconds.

Breaking news mid-segment. Producer in my ear saying go go go to the story I have not read yet. The package is loading on the screen and I have one line on a piece of paper and I am supposed to talk for forty seconds and I do not even know who the people in the story are.

Lost the field reporter. Lost his signal. He was about to deliver the lead and the satellite truck is showing no feed and the director is in my ear telling me to fill and I have no notes on the story and the camera is on me.

Wrong graphic. The graphic that just came up has the wrong name on it. The wrong name. I have to correct it on air without making it worse and the family of the person actually mentioned might be watching and I have eight seconds to figure out the wording.
Coughing fit. I cannot stop coughing. I am on camera and I am coughing into my sleeve and the producer is trying to find someone to throw to and I cannot speak and there is no break to cut to.

Guest is meltdown. The guest is screaming at the other guest and they are both standing and the moderator is trying to interrupt and the camera is wide and the network is going to see this and there is no commercial coming up for nine minutes.

Mic is hot during the toss. I just said something extremely candid about the segment producer and the mic was hot and the control room is silent and there is no way to retract it and the show is still on air.

Prompter died. Whole prompter went dark and I am improvising and the script was twelve paragraphs of detailed quote attribution and now I am trying to remember which side said what and the seconds are ticking and the executive producer is pacing behind the cameras.

Earpiece keeps dropping. I am missing every cue. I cannot tell when to throw to break and I just talked over the bumper music and the audio guy is sprinting across the studio with a backup pack and the camera does not stop.

Camera went dead on a two-shot and the live audience is staring and the host is staring and I am the floor director and I have to get a working camera up in the next four seconds and the only spare is on the wrong lens.

Water in the cabin. Water in the CABIN. The hull is breached. The bilge pump is running but losing and the swim ladder is gone and the radio is just static and I am scanning the horizon for any other boat.

Mayday. Mayday mayday. Channel 16. I am yelling into the radio and the Coast Guard is asking for my position and the GPS just died and I am reading the chartplotter as it loses screen brightness from the water.
Hit something. Hit something hard. The bow is taking on water and we are going down by the bow and I am running for the life raft and the painter is tangled and I cannot get the raft over the rail.

Engine fire. Engine room is on fire and the smoke is filling the cabin and the kids are below and I am screaming for them to come up and the smoke detector is shrieking and the fire extinguisher is somewhere on the deck and I cannot remember where.
Capsized. We rolled. The boat rolled in the swell and we are in the water and the boat is upside down and the dinghy is somewhere and I am counting heads. One. Two. Three. WHERE IS THE FOURTH.

Lifejacket is not inflating. The CO2 cartridge must be empty. I am pulling the manual tube and blowing into it and my lungs are full of saltwater and there is a wave coming and I am not strong enough to fight it.

Storm came up fast. Wind shifted ninety degrees and the chop is breaking over the gunwales and the bilge alarm is on and I have one hand on the helm trying to point into the waves and one hand on the radio mic.

Reef. We are on the reef. Hit it at six knots and the bottom is grinding and the keel is groaning and water is coming up through the floorboards and the tide is going out which means we are stuck and the boat is going to keel over.

Man overboard. Man overboard. I hit the MOB button and I have one hand on the wheel and I am circling back and the wake is white and I lost sight of him for two seconds and he is in a wetsuit and the swell is six feet.

EPIRB. Activate the EPIRB. Pulled the lanyard and the strobe is going and I am hoping someone gets the signal and the boat is listing thirty degrees and the kids are in life jackets clipped to the jackline and I am throwing flares.

Six tickets in three minutes. Three. The line is buried and the duck is not resting and the runner is asking where the asparagus is and the asparagus is still in the walk-in and I have not made the mother sauce and table four sent something back.

Salamander broke. The salamander broke and I have eight steaks to finish and the broilers are full and I am improvising with a torch and the torch is running out of butane and the table is waiting and the GM is in the kitchen which never happens at this hour.

Saucier just cut himself. Bad. Blood everywhere on the station. I am pulling him off the line and tying off the bleed and the printer is still spitting tickets and pasta is on the fire and the sauce is about to break.

VIP. VIP on table eleven. Critic. Critic in the dining room. The expo is whispering it down the line and now every hand is shaking and the chef de cuisine is staring at the pass and the plate I just sent has a thumb print on the rim.

Eighty-six the scallops. Eighty-six the scallops. We are out and the floor still has the dish on the menu and the table just ordered three and the manager is at the pass and the supplier cannot deliver until tomorrow.

Walk-in is warm. Walk-in is WARM. The compressor died sometime in the last hour and the protein is at fifty-two and the line is in the weeds and we need to figure out what is salvageable and what gets eighty-sixed and the temperature is still climbing.

Allergy ticket. Severe shellfish allergy on table fourteen with the linguine. The linguine has shrimp stock in it. The stock pot has been used for everything tonight. I have to start a fresh pot and the table is on a fifteen minute clock.

Fire on the line. The grease in the fryer caught and the flames are at the hood and the suppression system has not triggered and the fire extinguisher is at the back of the kitchen and the diners can see into the kitchen through the pass.

Dishwasher quit. Walked out in the middle of service. The bus tubs are stacking and we have no clean plates for the next course and the dining room is full and the bartender is on the phone trying to find anyone available who can come in tonight.

Pass is twelve plates deep. Twelve. I am calling out tickets and nobody is hearing me and the sous is on his phone and the lamb is going to pass medium and table six just got the wrong appetizer and they are sending it back.

Other car is in the ditch. The driver is slumped over the wheel. I am running across the lanes and the windshield is spider-webbed and there is steam coming up and I am pulling at the door handle and the door will not open and I can see he is not moving.
Three-car pileup. The car behind me hit me and I hit the car in front and now the car behind me is on fire and I am trying to get my seatbelt off and the buckle is jammed and the door is crumpled.

Smell of gas. Strong. After the crash the smell of gas is everywhere and I am dragging my passenger out by the shoulders and the door is half-open and the engine is ticking and there are sparks somewhere I cannot see.
Pinned. My leg is pinned under the dash. I cannot move. I cannot see down to it. I am calling out and the ambulance is on the way and I do not know how bad it is and I am terrified to look.

Baby is crying in the back. The car seat is intact and the baby is crying which is good but I cannot turn around because my neck. My neck. I cannot turn my neck. And the other driver is at my window screaming at me.

Highway shoulder. I am standing on the highway shoulder waving at oncoming cars and the wrecked car is in the middle lane and the driver is unconscious and the next car is going to hit it if I cannot get them to slow.

Hit and run. The car that hit me just drove off. I am bleeding from a cut on my head and the back of my car is folded and I am trying to read the license plate from memory and I only got three digits.

Cyclist. We hit a cyclist. He is on the pavement and he is not moving and the helmet is cracked and people are getting out of their cars and someone is screaming and I am trying to dial nine-one-one and my hands are shaking so bad I keep hitting the wrong numbers.

Truck jackknifed in front of us. Brakes locked. Tires screaming. Hit it. Hit the side of the trailer at forty miles an hour and the airbags went off and the dust is white in the cabin and I cannot tell if my kid in the back seat is okay.

Black ice. The car is sliding sideways and the guardrail is coming and we are going to roll. We are going to ROLL. Bracing. Bracing. The world is turning over and over and I do not know how to stop my head from hitting the window.

Engine just failed. Right engine. The plane is yawing and the captain is on the rudder and the warning horn is going and the passengers are looking at the wing and the wing has a smoke trail behind it.

Cabin pressure. Oxygen masks dropped. The masks dropped over every seat and the captain is announcing rapid descent and my ears are popping and the baby in the row ahead is screaming and the mother cannot get her mask on first because the baby is screaming.

Turbulence severe. Severe. The plane just dropped what felt like a hundred feet and the carts hit the ceiling and the flight attendants are on the floor and the captain is yelling on the PA to stay seated and a man two rows behind me is shouting that he is having a heart attack.

Smoke in the cabin. Real smoke. People are coughing and the lights have gone to dim emergency and the captain is asking flight attendants to prepare for emergency landing and we are over water and I cannot tell where the nearest airport is.

Bird strike. Both engines surged at takeoff and the plane is climbing slow and the captain is on the radio with the tower and the wings are level but the airspeed is bleeding and we cleared the runway by twenty feet.

Brace for impact. The captain just said brace for impact. Brace for impact. I am bent forward with my head on the seat in front of me and the flight attendants are shouting commands and I do not know what we hit or what is happening or where we are.

Gear is not down. Gear indicator is showing red. The captain is doing another pass and the runway is below and the wheels are still up and the foam trucks are at the end of the runway and the passengers are silent and I can hear someone praying.

Emergency descent. Steep. We are dropping fast and my stomach is in my throat and the oxygen mask is fogged and the cabin altitude warning is sounding and a flight attendant just lost her footing and went down hard.

Lost a passenger. Medical. Heart attack in row 22. The flight attendants are doing compressions in the aisle and the AED is hooked up and the captain is diverting to the nearest field and we are still forty minutes out.

Aborted takeoff. We were doing 120 knots and the captain slammed on the brakes and now the brakes are smoking and the plane is veering and there are fire trucks at the end of the runway already moving and the cabin smells like burning rubber.

Three down. Three down at the corner of the building. I am running with the kit and the rounds are still coming in over my head and the corpsman is yelling for cover and the first guy is bleeding from the femoral and I have ten seconds before he is gone.

Tourniquet on. Tourniquet ON. Cranking. Cranking until the windlass locks. The leg is white below the knee. The bleeding stopped. Next. Move to the next patient. Where is the next patient. Behind the wall. Drag him. Drag him.

Chest wound. Sucking chest wound. Air going in and out of the hole and I am tearing the seal package open and slapping it on and the patient is panicking and I cannot get him to lie still and the medevac is twelve minutes out.

Mass casualty. We have eight casualties in the courtyard and three of us. The lieutenant is yelling for triage tags and I am sorting and tagging and someone is screaming for his mother and I cannot save him, I have to move past him, the next one might live.

Airway. Airway is closed. He is gasping and his lips are blue and I am cricking the head back and the jaw is rigid and I am reaching for the NPA and the NPA is in my other bag and the other bag is across the road.

Tension pneumo. Side of the chest is bulging and the trachea is shifted. Needle decompression. Where is the needle. Right intercostal space. Counting ribs. Counting through gloves. There. Pop. Air rushing out. Saturation coming back.

IV will not start. Veins are flat. He is bled out enough that the veins collapsed and I have a peripheral kit and the IO drill in my pack and I am drilling the humerus and the patient is unconscious and the next round is coming in over the wall.

Bird is six minutes. Six minutes. Patient is in shock, BP barely palpable, IV running wide open with fluids and the fluids are not catching up to the bleed and we cannot stop all of it and the helicopter is six minutes and he might not have six minutes.

Second tourniquet. Need a second tourniquet. The first one is on the thigh and the bleeding shifted to the calf and I am out of tourniquets. I am out. I am using a belt and torquing it with a pen and watching the bleeding slow.

He is asking if he is going to make it. I cannot tell him. I cannot tell him yes or no and his hand is gripping mine and I am pretending to look at his bandage to avoid his eyes and the medevac is inbound and the LZ is not secure.

Caterer just called. Caterer just called and said they double-booked and they cannot do our wedding tonight. Tonight. Two hundred guests in seven hours and no food and the venue does not allow outside catering except through approved vendors and the list of approved vendors is on the planner's laptop and the planner is not picking up.

Dress has a stain. Right down the front of the bodice. Foundation. I just put on makeup and brushed the dress and now the dress has makeup on it and the photographer is here in thirty minutes and the seamstress is two hours away.

DJ is sick. Sick. He just texted. The DJ for my wedding tonight is sick. He cannot do it. He is sending a sub but the sub does not have my song list and the song list has my parents' first dance and the surprise song for the bridal party and the ceremony cues.

Cake is wrong. The cake is wrong. The baker delivered a cake that is the wrong shape and the wrong color and the wrong filling and the cake is in the lobby and I have ninety minutes to get it fixed or replaced and the baker is not answering.

It is raining. POURING. The ceremony is outdoors. The tents are not coming until five and the ceremony is at four and the chairs are getting soaked and the florist is trying to move the arch and the arch is too heavy and the ground is mud.

Best man lost the rings. Lost them. He had them this morning and now they are not in his pocket and we have searched the hotel room and the lobby and the parking lot and the ceremony starts in eighty-three minutes.

Bridesmaid did not show up. Has not answered her phone since last night. The procession is supposed to be even and now we are uneven and people are showing up and the photographer wants to do the group shots and we have an empty space where she should be.

Officiant cancelled. Family emergency. The officiant just texted that he cannot make it and we are scrambling to find a replacement and we have a wedding in five hours and you cannot get someone ordained that fast and the marriage certificate has his name on it.

Flowers wilted. The flowers were stored overnight in a warm room and the bouquets are drooping and the centerpieces are brown around the edges and the florist is forty-five minutes out and the photos start in an hour.

Groom is having a meltdown. Locked himself in the bathroom and is not answering and the best man is talking to him through the door and the ceremony is in two hours and the cars are arriving and the bride's mother is asking what is happening.

Dead air. Dead air just hit. The board went dark and the song stopped halfway through and the engineer is sprinting from the back and I am alone in the studio and the mic is hot and I have to say something and I cannot think of anything to say.

Caller is going off the rails. He just said a slur on air and the dump button is jammed and the seven-second delay is gone and the GM is going to fire me and the producer is making throat-cut signs and I am scrambling to cut to commercial.

Transmitter is down. Off the air for the last four minutes and the listeners are calling in on every line and the engineer is on the roof and the storm is over the tower and lightning is striking and the chief is screaming over the phone.

Cart machine just spat out a blank. I queued the spot and the spot played silent. Twenty seconds of silence on a national feed. I have to fill, I have to fill, I am riffing about the weather and my voice is shaking.

EAS tone. The Emergency Alert System tone just fired and I did not initiate it and I have no idea what alert it is. The screen is blank. The script printer is jammed. I have to read something on air and I do not have the something to read.

Lost the news feed. The wire is silent. I am supposed to read the top of the hour news in forty seconds and the printer has nothing and the website is loading and the deadline is closing and my heart is in my throat.

Wrong audio. The clip that just played was a different story than the one I introduced and the listeners are going to be confused and the program director is on line two and I have one minute to fix this before the next segment.

Generator failed. Building lost power and the generator did not kick on and we are on battery and we have maybe two minutes of battery and the morning show is in the middle of a sponsor read and I cannot tell them yet because that would be worse.

Hot mic. My co-host's mic is hot during the song and she is talking about a sponsor in extremely unflattering terms and the song is over in twelve seconds and I cannot get to her in time and the levels are showing her voice clearly.

Caller line is dead. The phone system crashed. I am supposed to do twenty minutes of talkback right now and there are no calls and the producer is across the hall trying to reboot the phone system and the dead air is filling and I am alone with a microphone.

Pallet is falling. Pallet is falling off the top rack and there is a worker below and I am screaming and waving and the worker is wearing earbuds and not turning and the pallet is tipping and going to come down right on him.

Forklift tipped. The forklift tipped on the loading dock and the operator went out the side and the cage was not down and the forks are pinning him to the pavement and we are running and trying to lift it and it is too heavy.

Rack just collapsed. Section three. The whole upright is bowing and the load is shifting and I am running people back and the boxes are falling in slow motion and I can hear the steel groaning and the sprinkler heads are vibrating.

Chemical spill. Acid drum tipped and the floor is steaming and the alarm is going and the supervisor is yelling for the spill kit and the spill kit is across the warehouse and I have to evacuate this aisle right now because the fumes are heavy.

Conveyor jammed and the belt is still trying to drive. The motor is whining and smoking and the operator's hand is caught in the rollers and I am hitting the emergency stop and the e-stop is not stopping it.

Trailer detached. Trailer detached from the truck and rolled backward into the loading bay and crushed the dock plate and there were two guys at the dock plate and now one of them is on the floor not moving and the other is screaming.

Truck rolled out without the chock. The driver is back at the cab and not paying attention and the truck is rolling slowly toward the open dock and there is no one between to stop it and the dock is fifteen feet to a drop.

Pallet of beverage glass just dropped from the forks at twelve feet. The glass is everywhere. Everywhere. A worker was walking past and got caught in the spray and there is blood and shouting and the floor is wet and someone is running for the first aid kit.

Battery acid leaking from the floor scrubber. The acid is reaching the drain and the drain runs to the storm system and I am running for the absorbent pads and the supervisor is on the phone with environmental and the timer on reporting just started.

Roof leak became a roof breach. Water and chunks of insulation pouring down on the inventory and the electrical panel is right under it and the sparks are starting and I am running for the breaker and someone is yelling to get out.
